items.title: Study finds 40,000-year-old carvings approach complexity of earliest writing

featured_image.name: 40,000-Year-Old Symbols Suggest Humans Created a ...

items.description: More than 40,000 years ago, Ice Age humans in Europe were carving patterns of dots, lines, and crosses into tools and ivory figurines — and a new study finds those markings were far from random. A computational analysis of more than 3,000 such symbols, published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), concludes that the engravings display a level of complexity and information density comparable to proto-cuneiform, the earliest known writing system that emerged in Mesopotamia around 3,000 B.C.E. The findings arrive alongside a separate study, published in Science Advances, that pushes the oldest known Homo erectus fossils in eastern Asia back to 1.77 million years ago. Together, the two papers reshape longstanding assumptions about when early humans began encoding information and how rapidly our ancestors spread across the globe.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Study links Saturn's rings to ancient crash that formed Titan

featured_image.name: Saturn's rings may have formed after a huge collision with Titan

items.description: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, and its spectacular ring system may both owe their existence to a single cataclysmic event — a collision between two ancient moons roughly 400 million years ago, according to a study led by SETI Institute scientist Matija Ćuk. The research, posted to the preprint server arXiv on February 11 and accepted for publication in The Planetary Science Journal, presents computer simulations suggesting the crash reshaped much of the Saturnian system.[1][2]

items.title: Study: climate policies averted 3B tons of CO2 in 2022

featured_image.name: Assessing 2025 NDCs | World Resources ...

items.description:
Countries that adopt stricter and better-targeted climate policies are cutting carbon emissions faster, according to what researchers describe as the most comprehensive analysis of global climate policy ever assembled. The study, published Monday in Nature Communications, analyzed more than 3,900 policies enacted since 2000 across 43 leading economies responsible for more than three-quarters of global emissions.[1][2]

By comparing present-day emissions with a scenario in which no climate policies existed, the international research team found that existing policies avoided an estimated 3.1 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2022 alone — roughly equal to the European Union's entire annual output.[3][2][4]

items.title: Asian stocks climb as Wall Street tech rebound eases AI fears

featured_image.name: Asia-Pacific markets set to open mixed as gold hits fresh record of $5,000

items.description:
Asian markets opened higher on Wednesday as a tech-driven rebound on Wall Street eased fears about the disruptive effects of artificial intelligence that had rattled global equities earlier in the week. The gains came ahead of Nvidia's closely watched quarterly earnings report, due later Wednesday, and as investors digested President Donald Trump's State of the Union address delivered Tuesday evening.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index extended its advance to a third consecutive day, according to Bloomberg, with shares rising across Japan, South Korea, and Australia. Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed around 1% in early trading, while South Korea's Kospi also gained approximately 1%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 opened nearly 1% higher. In mainland China, the Shanghai Composite rose for a second straight session, climbing about 0.5%, with technology and AI-related stocks leading the advance.[1][2][3]

items.title: HSBC's 2025 profit beats estimates despite $5B in charges

featured_image.name: HSBC: Bank's pre-tax profits soar fuelled by high interest rates

items.description:
HSBC, Europe's largest bank, on Wednesday reported annual pretax profit of $29.9 billion for 2025, a 7.4 percent decline from $32.3 billion the previous year, as nearly $5 billion in one-off charges weighed on results. The figure nonetheless exceeded the $28.9 billion analyst consensus compiled by Bloomberg, buoyed by strong performance in wealth management and transaction banking.[1][2]

"2025 was a year of decisive action and swift execution, which is reflected in our strong performance," Group CEO Georges Elhedery said in the bank's earnings release. Revenue rose 4 percent to $68.3 billion, while profit excluding notable items climbed to $36.6 billion from $34.2 billion, underscoring the health of the bank's underlying operations.[3][1]

items.title: Gold tops $5,200 as new U.S. tariffs take effect amid trade chaos

featured_image.name: Gold hits three-week high as U.S. tariff ruling incites safe-haven buying

items.description: Gold prices climbed to a three-week high this week as investors poured into safe-haven assets following a sudden upheaval in U.S. trade policy. The rally was triggered by the Supreme Court's decision on Friday to strike down President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs, and then his rapid imposition of new levies under a different legal authority, injecting fresh uncertainty into global markets.

items.title: Mexico probes cartel-linked accounts spreading fake news after El Mencho killing

featured_image.name: After killing of top drug lord, cartels use fake news to spread fear in Mexico

items.description:
When the Mexican army killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes — the fugitive cartel leader known as "El Mencho" — during a military operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco, on Sunday, February 22, genuine violence rippled across western Mexico. But researchers say a coordinated propaganda campaign by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel simultaneously manufactured a far more apocalyptic picture online, flooding social media with fabricated images and false reports designed to amplify fear and undermine confidence in the Mexican government.[1][2][3][4]

Among the debunked claims: assassins had seized Guadalajara's airport, a plane was ablaze on the runway, smoke was billowing from a church and buildings in Puerto Vallarta, American tourists were being held hostage, and armed groups had attacked civilians at the airport. The Mexico Embassy in the United States issued a point-by-point rebuttal on X, labeling each claim false. A fact-check by Lead Stories found that the viral image of a burning aircraft was almost certainly generated by artificial intelligence, with the Hive Moderation detection tool rating it 93.2 percent likely to be AI-created. Telltale signs included gibberish text on boarding stairs, mismatched aircraft windows, and a figure standing implausibly close to the flames.[3][5][6]

items.title: Bitcoin miners liquidate reserves, pivot to AI as prices plunge

featured_image.name: Bitcoin falls below $65,000 as Trump tariff moves raise uncertainty

items.description:
Bitcoin has fallen more than 26% year-to-date, logging its worst start to a year on record and its weakest consecutive monthly performance since the 2022 crypto winter. The decline, compounded by President Donald Trump's announcement of a 15% global tariff on imports that took effect February 24, has pushed mining operations to breakeven or below, forcing companies across the sector to liquidate reserves and accelerate their pivot away from cryptocurrency.[1][2][3][4]

The original cryptocurrency dropped below $65,000 on Monday after Trump's tariff announcement over the weekend sent shockwaves through global markets, according to CNBC. Bitcoin has now posted six consecutive negative weekly closes — a first in its history — and has fallen roughly 47% from its all-time high near $126,000 set in October.[5][6][4]

items.title: Russia accuses UK and France of plotting to arm Ukraine with nukes

featured_image.name: Russia accuses Ukraine of seeking to acquire nuclear weapon ...

items.description:
Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service on Tuesday accused Britain and France of secretly working to supply Ukraine with nuclear weapons, an allegation that drew swift denials from London, Paris, and Kyiv and prompted one of Moscow's most explicit nuclear threats since the full-scale invasion began four years ago.

The SVR, Russia's primary foreign intelligence agency, issued the claims on the fourth anniversary of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, asserting that London and Paris "are preparing to arm Kyiv with a nuclear bomb" because they believe conventional forces cannot defeat Russia. The agency provided no evidence to support its allegations.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: US warned Ukraine over strikes that hit American oil interests

featured_image.name: US warned Ukraine not to hit US interests in strikes on ...

items.description: Ukraine's ambassador to the United States disclosed on Tuesday that Washington delivered a formal diplomatic complaint after Ukrainian attacks on the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk damaged infrastructure tied to American oil investments in Kazakhstan, underscoring the complex intersection of the war with global energy interests.

items.title: Russia losing troops faster than it can replace them, Western officials say

featured_image.name: Russians 'being killed faster than Kremlin can recruit them'

items.description:
On the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western officials disclosed that Moscow's battlefield losses have outpaced its ability to recruit replacements for three consecutive months, a development that could reshape the trajectory of the conflict.

Since November, Russian forces have suffered nearly 40,000 casualties per month while managing to enlist only about 35,000 new troops, according to Western officials cited by The Telegraph. The growing deficit marks what analysts describe as a potential turning point in Europe's largest land war since 1945.[1][2]

items.title: Russia opens criminal case against Telegram's Durov

featured_image.name: Telegram CEO says French charges against him are ‘misguided' — read his full statement

items.description:
Russia has launched a criminal investigation into Pavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of Telegram, on charges of facilitating terrorist activities, the state-run newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported on Tuesday, citing evidence from the Federal Security Service (FSB). The move marks a sharp escalation in Moscow's increasingly confrontational campaign against the messaging platform and its Dubai-based founder.

"The actions of the head of Telegram, P. Durov, are being investigated as part of a criminal case on the grounds of a crime under Part 1.1 of Article 205.1 (assistance to terrorist activities) of the Criminal Code of Russia," Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported in an article it said was "based on materials from the FSB of Russia." The charge carries a potential sentence of eight years to life imprisonment.[1][2][3]

Durov responded to the announcement on his Telegram channel. "Russia has opened a criminal case against me for aiding terrorism," he wrote, describing the investigation as pressure on the messenger service.[4]

items.title: US and NATO launch major Arctic exercises amid rising tensions

featured_image.name: NORAD and NORTHCOM Initiate Arctic Edge 2026 Multi ...

items.description: The Arctic has emerged as a theater of intensifying military competition and environmental upheaval, with NATO launching new operations, the United States conducting exercises spanning Alaska and Greenland, and Russia and China deepening their joint presence across the region — all as record-breaking warmth reshapes the polar landscape.

items.title: King's College London creates first-ever aluminum compound to rival platinum catalysts

featured_image.name: Scientists create sustainable and cheaper catalysts from ...

items.description:
Chemists at King's College London have isolated a new form of aluminum that could offer a cheaper and more sustainable alternative to precious metals widely used in industrial catalysis. The work, led by Dr. Clare Bakewell, a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Chemistry, describes the first-ever cyclotrialumane — a compound made of three aluminum atoms arranged in a triangular structure — capable of breaking apart tough chemical bonds.[1][2]

Published in Nature Communications, the research comes at a time when supply chain disruptions and soaring costs for precious metals like platinum and palladium are forcing the chemical industry to search for abundant alternatives.[3][4]

items.title: U.S. details alleged secret Chinese nuclear test, urges disarmament talks

featured_image.name: US accuses China of increasing its nuclear arsenal - Le Monde

items.description: A senior American arms control official on Monday presented newly declassified details of what Washington says was a secret Chinese underground nuclear test conducted in 2020, urging the international community to pressure Beijing and Moscow toward nuclear disarmament just weeks after the last remaining U.S.-Russia arms treaty expired.

items.title: Meta signs 6-gigawatt AI chip deal with AMD

featured_image.name: AMD and Oracle announce agreement for 50,000 GPUs as AI deal ...

items.description:
Meta Platforms and AMD on Tuesday announced a multi-year, multi-generation agreement to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPUs for Meta's AI infrastructure, in a deal that could generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue for the chipmaker and reshape the competitive landscape of the AI hardware market.[1][2]

The partnership marks Meta's most direct move yet to diversify its AI compute supply chain beyond Nvidia, which secured its own sweeping deal with Meta just one week earlier. Under the agreement, AMD issued Meta a performance-based warrant for up to 160 million shares of AMD common stock — roughly 10% of the company — structured to vest as shipment milestones and stock price thresholds are achieved.[3][4][2]

items.title: Russia warns US nuclear testing would trigger 'domino effect'

featured_image.name: Putin issues nuclear warning to the West over strikes on ...

items.description: The United States on Monday doubled down on accusations that China conducted a secret underground nuclear test in 2020, presenting what it called newly declassified intelligence at the United Nations Conference on Disarmament in Geneva as it pushed for broader multilateral arms control negotiations.

items.title: Iran nears deal to buy supersonic missiles from China

featured_image.name: Tracking the rapid US military build-up near Iran - Al Jazeera

items.description: Iran is close to finalizing an agreement with China to purchase CM-302 supersonic anti-ship cruise missiles, according to a Reuters report citing six people with knowledge of the negotiations. The deal would represent one of the most advanced military transfers between the two countries and comes as the United States positions a vast naval force near Iran's coastline amid escalating tensions over Tehran's nuclear program.[1]

items.title: Oil tanker costs hit 6-year high as US-Iran war fears mount

featured_image.name: Oil's $25 War Premium on Iran-Israel Risk Can Rapidly Fizzle Out

items.description: Oil prices are hovering near seven-month highs and the cost of chartering supertankers has tripled since the start of the year as the threat of military conflict between the United States and Iran rattles global energy markets. The surge reflects a deepening risk premium across the oil supply chain, driven not by actual supply losses but by the prospect of disruption to the world's most critical crude chokepoint.

items.title: Asian markets split as AI fears, new tariffs rattle investors

featured_image.name: EU pauses U.S. trade deal as it seeks clarity over Trump's new 15% global tariffs

items.description:
Asian stocks diverged on Tuesday as markets across the region absorbed a sharp Wall Street selloff driven by fresh concerns about artificial intelligence displacing legacy businesses, while a new 10% global tariff imposed by President Donald Trump took effect just days after the Supreme Court struck down his original trade duties.

Japan's Nikkei 225 surged 0.9% to 57,354 as markets reopened from a holiday, lifted by gains in semiconductor-related stocks. South Korea's Kospi climbed 1.8% to a record 5,951.90, powered by Samsung Electronics, which jumped 3.2%, and SK Hynix, up 4.8%. Mainland China also rallied on its return from Lunar New Year, with the Shanghai Composite rising 1.2%. But Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.9% to 26,564 as traders locked in profits from a recent rally.[1][2][3]
